Why medical students aren't matching in residency positions: an interesting article from the AMA

This isn't just an issue isolated to the medical field of education. I'm seeing people come out of universities with Engineering degrees or Business degrees with no experience, no back up plan and no idea what their standards should be when it comes to breaking into the industry.

As much as there isn't as many jobs anymore, there are still a lot of people who have unrealistic expectations about what they get after they graduate. Its made worse for MD's because they HAVE to do these residencies to finalize their education.

I completely agree. The other thing that makes it worse for MDs is these aren't normal job interviews. There is an interview season and everyone finds out the same day if they got a job and where, there is some chances to fill open positions at this point but not many. If you don't match you essentially have to wait an entire year. Having just gone through this I feel like everyone I know who didn't match had multiple negatives from that list against them. Universities, administrators, advisers, etc all need to start being more honest with everyone about what their goals should be regardless of field and people need to be more realistic with themselves.

Yeah, its getting to a weird cultural point in education. They are being shielded from high school into expecting certain things if they do a medical degree.

Did you manage to get matched? I didn't know that was the way they did things, thanks for the insight. What kind of negatives did these people have? Was it things like bad grades or terrible interviewing skills, or was it not being open minded about where they could work? I don't know much about the medical doctor system, so this all seems rather bizzare.

Yeah I matched. Honestly, I was a pretty strong candidate for my field. Different specialties are more competitive than others, and most of it boils down to earning potential and lifestyle. Dermatology for example is like a 9-5 M-F job and you make a lot of money, but family medicine usually is closer to a 6a-6p M-F, work a few hours on the weekend and the compensation isn't as great. Some people just want to do family though regardless of if they were "competitive" enough to do another field. Most of the ones I know who didn't match weren't as competitive in their field as they thought. A lot of that has to do with your USMLE scores (also called "boards" and "steps1-3") but also has to do with research, experience in medical school, etc. They also didn't have very good back up plans or apply to enough programs (more programs you apply to, hopefully means you you get more interviews, hopefully to increase the odds you match at one).

Wow, they sound like the type of people who, if they were engineers or IT professionals, would only stay in one industry or only learn one coding language, and refuse to travel to sites that needed work. I've met plenty of people like that.

And it's strange they didn't apply to more programs. Is the application process difficult, or was it more a result of their laziness? I mean fuck, when I was looking for a job I would apply to places I didn't even think would need me (and often those are places with jobs)

I think it is a little different for us, especially because it costs money to apply to these programs. When I say not enough I mean like the applied to 50 when they should applied to like 70, which is what you have to do for some of these specialties. Then you have to try to schedule your interviews, which involve a great deal of travel and again money, to fit their schedule. A back up plan involves applying to another specialty and doing all of those interviews too. It really just secondary to them having a strong desire to do a particular specialty but not have the test scores or resume to be able to do it. It sucks but I just don't think people were honest enough with them to say "Look I know you really want to do this but it is not going to happen"

The problem in medical "education" is that internship and residency are considered part of the "educational process". My this I mean that in the US, the interns and residents are sometimes unshielded and unprotected by federal or state laws in employment. Hospitals across this nation use interns and residents as a cheap labor source. They are not cheap labor and should be paid accordingly.

These newly graduated medical students have student debt and are often working in the most impoverished areas of the nation. Substantial debt forgiveness should be a part of the process of taking jobs in the inner cities as interns and residents.

More important for the purposes of the match, the AMA needs to disclose the ranking of the medical schools where these unmatched students came from and to what specialities they were applying. If there is a good relationship between the student and their school's professionals, then the students should be counseled and assisted.

Unfortunately, I am also aware of a few medical schools where unfortunate circumstances damage the student's career. Those circumstances are typically due to malfeasance, corruption, or misbehavior by medical center staff, medical school administrators, and/or professors at those schools. In one case, with which I am personally familiar, there was disciplinary action by the federal government on that school due to bias at the school. State officials later sanctioned the school and forced a change in their board of directors and leadership due to false statements to state regulators, necessitating a review by the state attorney general. Due to the local political strength of that school, the medical officials at the school were protected for many years until the disciplinary action forced the leadership change.

These types of things occur all the time in multiple states, multiple hospitals, and multiple medical centers/schools. The circumstances which I am referring to above occurred many many years back and are not a current investigation.

Sadly, they occur more often now due to the increasingly political environment of medical education funding and medical contracting for hospitals.

Okay, so feel free to poke all manner of holes into my argument but I see this as Obama "asking" the monied interests to stand down the lobbying in order to find some manner of tax that would allow for wealth distribution to the poorest. At heart, if those with the capital don't want such legislation to go through, it won't as a result of money=speech.
That said I would also propose this is filler; if the current administration wanted to make the poor a priority it sure as hell waited long enough to pull the card out.

The thing is, though, that the poor and middle class pay a higher percentage of their income than the rich, despite higher tax brackets. And the reason for this is that rich people are either really good at avoiding taxes or have enough money to hire people who are really good at avoiding taxes. So the 'fair share' is really just the same proportion that the middle class is paying.

Plus all big business and big industry is highly subsidized right down to the most base level. The fact industry pays half for electricity what consumers do is such a given it isn't even considered a subsidy, for example.

Eh, that's a bit too much of a blanket there. There are people who pay 0% income tax (but of course do pay other taxes like sales), but are you saying that they are paying a higher % than a person paying 50% of their income? I don't think that is the case.

Dollar wise, the rich do pay more although they are of course left with more too.
No one is paying 50% of their income. No one.

Do the math and you may be surprised. Top income tax bracket is 39.6%. Include 10% sales tax (CA), property tax, fees (car registration), additional taxes for certain goods (e.g. alcohol, gasoline) and we can be nearly certain that people are paying 50% of their income back to the government as a tax burden.
Poor, working poor and the middle class pay that much, the rich pay far far less and that my friend that is the problem.

On average, the extremely rich pay a lower percentage than the middle class and moderately poor (obviously not people earning minimum wage), because the rich store their money in tax havens and find other loopholes.

Also it's 50% of their income above a certain amount, not 50% of their total.

On average, the extremely rich pay a lower percentage

Of what? Of their income? Capital gains tax would be really the only way that would happen, and it accounts for far less income proportionally than typical forms (e.g. salary). Back this up with the math if you think it's incorrect.

Also it's 50% of their income above a certain amount, not 50% of their total.

Yes, that's called a progressive tax structure. They are taxed as they reach each lower level as well, but since those numbers are much lower, they become decreasingly less a proportion of their tax burden as income increases. This is to say nothing of the other taxation I discussed (sales tax for instance).

But really, this is not a matter of opinion: this is verifiable with math. Do the math on a person who earns $5million in taxable income according to the us tax code. You will see what they are paying in income tax. I am not defending the rich, nor am I rich myself, I just would rather deal with the fact of the matter than vaguely vilifying people.

What about the people that literally do NOTHING to EARN their money, other than have some other person move it around for them (hedge fund managers)? They have no work ethic and MASSIVE paychecks for doing nothing more than telling the financial manager to make a profit on their money.

Do you think that they should not have to pay even a small percentage for the extraordinary level of privilege that their birth brought them?

I think that should have to pay 50%, and all they have to do to break even is have their hedge fund manager or trader work a little bit harder for his 2 or 3 billion a year.
http://www.forbes.com/hedge-fund-managers/

No argument on the people born into wealth: when that is a person as you described (which is often is) that is a person society should not be producing.

However in the case of the fund managers you listed, many of those people are extremely hard workers who have done a great deal of good work in their lives and careers. For instance James Simmons. I am not for or against the wealthy as a class or group, but I am for work (as I take it you are as well based on your first comment). The latter group you vilify do work very hard and while we can debate the relative merit of their career choice, I don't think they should be derided as a group.
I have a hard time justifying a billion dollar a year salary, perhaps for solving world hunger, or curing cancer, but for shuffling other people's money around? Ya, that's a tough one.

you say they are doing nothing, but they are doing a huge service to some people: they are helping make a few people a lot of money, or helping a lot of people to make a lot of money.
